stem:
Consider this rule:
If a form is complete, it is accepted.

Which statement means exactly the same as this rule?
choices: If a form is not accepted, it is not complete.
If a form is accepted, it is complete.
If a form is not complete, it is not accepted.
If a form is complete, it is not accepted.
answer: If a form is not accepted, it is not complete.
hints: Only one way of rewriting an if-then rule keeps its meaning. It swaps the two parts and puts "not" in both.
Name the parts. If-part: the form is complete. Then-part: it is accepted.
Swap the if-part and the then-part, and put "not" in both. Find the choice that makes both moves. Swapping without "not", or adding "not" without swapping, changes the meaning.

solution.methodName: Go forward, or flip and negate both parts

steps.action: Name the parts. If-part (p): the form is complete. Then-part (q): it is accepted.
The contrapositive swaps the parts and puts "not" in both: if not q, then not p. Here: if a form is not accepted, it is not complete.
steps.why: If every complete form is accepted, then a form that was not accepted cannot be complete. Both rules forbid the same thing: a complete form that is not accepted.

steps.action: "If a form is accepted, it is complete" only swaps the parts. This is the converse, and it is not the same.
steps.why: The rule allows an incomplete form to be accepted too. The converse would forbid that.

steps.action: "If a form is not complete, it is not accepted" only adds "not". This is the inverse. It is not the same either, for the same reason.
"If a form is complete, it is not accepted" goes against the rule.
The answer is "If a form is not accepted, it is not complete."

This is the converse: it only swaps the parts. The rule never says incomplete forms are refused. Counterexample: an incomplete form is accepted. The rule stays true, but this statement is false.
trapNotes.If a form is not complete, it is not acc: This is the inverse: it only adds "not". The rule says what happens to complete forms, not to incomplete ones. Counterexample: an incomplete form is accepted. The rule stays true, but this statement is false.
trapNotes.If a form is complete, it is not accepte: This says the opposite of the rule's then-part. Any complete form would break it, so it cannot mean the same thing.
